t: for there is no oath there at all. For he did not use an expression of an oath or curse or imprecation (Hilchot Shevuot 2:2).
neither mention of the Name nor a substitute. Unlike an oath, for which, to be liable to a sacrifice or lashes, he must mention one of the names of God or its substitutes (ibid. halakhah 4).
burnt offering... peace offerings or a meal offering. And these offerings come by vow or voluntary gift (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 14:1).
he is liable for their responsibility. That if the animal dies after he set it aside for the offering, he must bring another in its place (see also there, halakhot 4-5).
in Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot. Chapters 14-17; see also Hilchot Arachin VeCharamin 1:1.
any amount. A very small measure.
as it is said, "he shall not profane his word". This is the negative commandment that a person may not profane what he forbade himself by his speech.

he is not flogged until he eats an olive-sized amount. For the term "eating" means an olive-sized amount or more (see also Hilchot Shevuot 4:1), and nevertheless it is forbidden even in less than an olive-sized amount (ibid.).
they combine to an olive-sized amount. And if he ate half an olive-sized amount of this and half of that, he is flogged.

one who says, "These fruits are a korban upon me". This form of vow is called "hatpasah" (extension), in which he applies a prohibition to a certain item by virtue of an existing prohibition on another item (see below halakhot 13, 15). Here he intends to apply to the fruits a prohibition by virtue of the prohibition of eating an offering. In this way, if he transgresses his vow, he is liable for me'ilah (see Hilchot Me'ilah 4:9; see Meiri, Nedarim 2a, who cites a dispute among early authorities on whether a vow by extension is an additional kind of vow or all vows take effect by extension).
"whatever I eat with you is a korban upon me" etc.. His intention is to forbid himself to eat it with his fellow, as an offering.

because it is possible for a person to vow an offering and make an animal that was ordinary into a forbidden offering. For the extension of a prohibition in a vow takes effect only when he extends it by virtue of something that a person has the power to forbid to himself, as follows.
if that forbidden thing can be made by vow. Such as an offering, which a person can consecrate.
and if it cannot be made by vow. Such as carcasses and torn animals and the like, which are forbidden in themselves and not through the person.

these are permitted. The Sages learned this principle from the verse "When a man vows a vow" and explained that one must vow "on what can be vowed and not on what is forbidden" (Babylonian Talmud, Nedarim 14a); that is, extension of a vow takes effect only on something that a person can forbid to himself by a vow, but not on something whose prohibition is intrinsic and does not depend on a person's vow.
as will be explained in its place. Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 14:8.
the one who vows can bring them because of his vow. And therefore they are defined as something that can be made by vow.
for one who vows to be a nazirite brings a sin offering. As part of the offerings he brings when his days of naziriteship are complete (Hilchot Nezirut 8:1).
and if he became impure, he brings a guilt offering. As part of the offerings he brings after he is purified from corpse impurity (ibid. 6:11).
like the challah of Aaron. Like the challah separated from dough that is given to a kohen who is of the seed of Aaron.
or like his terumah. Terumah gedolah or terumat ma'aser, which is given to the kohen.

for there it is not the way to bring these by vow and voluntary gift. Although they are not forbidden in themselves but only through the person setting them aside, since terumot and ma'asrot are not things that come by vow and voluntary gift, they are not considered "something that can be made by vow."
like leftover. Meat remaining from the offering after the time when it may be eaten, which is forbidden to eat.

like piggul. An offering disqualified because the kohen intended to eat it outside its time or outside its place (in the general sense of the term "piggul"; see Rosh, Nedarim 10b), and it is forbidden to eat.
like impure meat of sacred offerings. An offering that became impure and is forbidden to eat.

for he made them like the meat of an offering in any case. Although these are considered "forbidden things," since before they became forbidden they were offerings, his intention is to extend his vow by virtue of an offering, which is "something that can be vowed," and therefore his vow takes effect (see a similar principle below, halakhah 15).
like the tithe of animals. A person is commanded to separate one tenth of all the animals born to him each year (Hilchot Bekhorot 6:1).

since its sanctity is in the hands of man. For the tithe is not sanctified until he sanctifies the tenth. (Although the tithe does not come by vow and voluntary gift, since it is a lesser sacred offering, which generally comes by vow and voluntary gift, the designation of the animal tithe is also considered "something that can be made by vow"; Netiv Meir, above halakhah 11; see also below 2:9.)
whose sanctity is not in the hands of man. For the firstborn is sanctified on its own upon leaving the womb (Hilchot Bekhorot 1:5), and therefore it is defined as a "forbidden thing."

and he cannot extend it by vow, for it says of it, "no man shall sanctify it". The Sages learned from this verse that after it has left its mother's womb it cannot be changed to another kind of consecration, and so from this side as well it cannot be defined as something that can be brought by vow (see Hilchot Temurah 4:11-12; Responsa Birkat Avraham no. 46).
like the cherem to heaven. Like consecrations that a person consecrates saying: "This is cherem to heaven."

for cherem to heaven is for the upkeep of the Temple. Meant for repairs of the Temple (see Hilchot Arachin VeCharamin 1:10), and one may not benefit from them as from consecrated property, unlike cherem of kohanim, which is the kohen's property, and therefore one who extends a vow by it is permitted (as below 2:8).
like the terumah of the chamber. The shekel money given in the chamber, from which communal offerings are bought (see Hilchot Shekalim 4:1).
like the tamidim. Like the daily tamid offering.
like the diriyim. Chambers in the Temple courts (Commentary to the Mishnah, Nedarim 1:3).
like the wood. The wood of the altar.
like the fires. The parts of offerings that are burned on the altar fire.
like the ya'im. Utensils with which the ashes are cleared from the altar.
like the mizrakot. Vessels in which the blood of the offerings is received in order to throw it on the altar.
like the forks. With which the offerings on the altar are turned over so that they burn properly.

for all these expressions mean the same as saying, "They are a korban upon me". And even when he says "like the Sanctuary" or "like Jerusalem," he means the offerings brought in the Sanctuary or in Jerusalem.
for it is permitted to non-kohanim. For it is permitted for Israelites to eat after the throwing of its blood.
these are forbidden. Although this meat in its present state is permitted to eat.
for he extended only to its essence, which was forbidden. His intention is to extend to the essence of the offering, which was forbidden before the throwing of the blood.

but if it was the meat of a firstborn, if before the throwing of the blood, it is forbidden. Although extension by a firstborn is not an extension (as above halakhah 13), that applies only before it is slaughtered; but here, where the meat of the firstborn lies before him awaiting the throwing of the blood and burning on the altar, one who says this is considered as extending by an offering generally, and it is forbidden (Radbaz; Responsa Birkat Avraham no. 46, cited in Kesef Mishneh).
and if after the throwing of the blood, it is permitted. For it has returned to being like an extension by its essence, and one who extends by a firstborn is permitted.

and just as he forbids himself by substitute terms, so if he consecrated by substitute terms it is consecrated. See Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 14:11. Likewise substitute terms for an oath are like an oath (Hilchot Shevuot 2:5), and substitute terms for naziriteship are like naziriteship (Hilchot Nezirut 1:8).

and a substitute for substitutes is permitted. That is, he makes a variant of the words that are substitutes for offering, such as saying "mekanmena," "mekanchena," "mekansena," or other expressions built on the substitutes, such as with cherem when he says "charafim," "charakim," "charakhim" (Babylonian Talmud, Nedarim 10b).
dechei. Pure (in Aramaic).

it is as if he said to him, "What I eat of yours shall not be ordinary food but an offering". Its meaning is that what I eat of yours will be forbidden to me as an offering, and therefore I will not eat of yours (Radbaz; and similarly below halakhah 21).

"the korban that I eat of yours," "korban I eat of yours," "like the korban I eat of yours" is forbidden. For when he says "that I eat of yours" in connection with these expressions, the meaning is that what I eat of yours will be forbidden to me like an offering (Commentary to the Mishnah, Nedarim 1:4).
"not korban, I will not eat of yours". The meaning of his words is that because of the offering I will not eat anything of yours (Commentary to the Mishnah, ibid.).

for the meaning of these words is not etc.. For his words can be interpreted as swearing by the life of the offering that he will not eat of his fellow, and because this is not the language of an oath he is not liable for an oath; or the words can be interpreted as a vow not to eat his fellow's offering, and there is no vow here because one cannot vow regarding an act but only regarding an object (as below 3:1).
it is permitted. For in all these expressions it implies that he is extending his eating of his fellow's food by ordinary food, and there is no prohibition here.
for its meaning is that what I eat will be piggul or impure, therefore I will not eat of yours. As if he said: I will not eat of yours because what I eat of yours will be impure, and the like.
"like the Sanctuary that I eat of yours"... is forbidden. Since he said "that I eat of yours," it means that what I eat of yours will be forbidden to me like the Sanctuary.

for this is like one who swore by the Sanctuary that he will not eat. For the expression "that I will not eat of yours" is used in an oath, and this is not oath language. Likewise if he said "the Sanctuary, I will not eat of yours" or "by the Sanctuary I will not eat of yours" and the like, it is permitted because this is the language of an oath (as above halakhah 19; Radbaz; see Kesef Mishneh, who explained otherwise and emended the text of the Rambam).
the meaning of this is that he will not speak with him. His intention is to forbid his mouth to speak with him and the like (as below 3:10-11; Chazon Ish, Yoreh De'ah 142:4).
meshamtana mimcha. An expression of ban (Hilchot Talmud Torah 7:2). One under a ban may not sit within four cubits of others (ibid. halakhah 4).
and if he ate, he is not flogged. Because he expressed himself in the language of a ban, which is not the language of a vow, he is not flogged for it.
"It is upon me like the vows of the wicked" etc.. For the wicked are accustomed to vow and swear in a moment of anger and the like.
for among their vows are nazirite, offering and oath. These are the words of the one making the vow, and this expression obligates him in all that he took upon himself if he eats.

he is liable for all of them. He becomes a nazirite and must bring to the Temple an offering that comes by vow (a burnt offering or peace offering; Meiri, Nedarim 2a), and he is also liable to lashes for violating an oath of utterance (see also Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 14:11).

"like the voluntary gifts of the righteous" etc.. For it is the way of the righteous to bring the offering to the Temple court and donate it there (Commentary to the Mishnah, Nedarim 1:1). Therefore when he said "like the voluntary gifts of the righteous if I eat of yours" and he ate, he became liable for what he said.
for among their voluntary gifts are nazirite and offering. But not an oath, since it is not the way of the righteous to swear (see Hilchot Shevuot 12:12).

he said, "It is upon me like the vows of the wicked" etc.. In this case, where he did not say the ending "for among their vows are nazirite, offering and oath," he does not intend to obligate himself in an offering if he eats, but to forbid eating his fellow's food by extension to an offering, and the prohibition takes effect even though he did not say explicitly "the offering that I eat of yours" and the like (Lechem Mishneh; Me'iri Ha-Kesef).

he said, "like the vows of the righteous," he did not become liable for anything. For there is no obligating vow language here, so if he said "It is upon me like the vows of the righteous if I eat of yours," he is not forbidden to eat his fellow's food, and likewise if he concluded and said "for among their vows are nazirite and offering," he is not obligated in them.

for the righteous do not vow in a manner of prohibition and anger. The righteous do not act rashly and carelessly out of anger, and therefore they do not obligate themselves by a vow, since a vow carries responsibility (as above halakhah 2) and by it they might come to violate "do not delay" (Commentary to the Mishnah, Nedarim 1:1).
and a nazirite was passing before him. For if no nazirite is passing before him, his words "I am" can be interpreted as a fast.
"like the vows of the wicked, upon me," he is liable for an offering. Even though no animal is passing before him, since his words have no other meaning (Radbaz).
that I will not eat of it. Of a certain loaf.
he is liable for an oath like one who vows. He becomes liable for an oath, like the wicked who vow and obligate themselves by an oath.
he said nothing. Because his intention was the parchments (see also Hilchot Shevuot 12:4).
so that they do not treat vows lightly. So that they do not make light of vows (see also below 2:12-13).
for in it is written "prohibition and vow". And he is like one who vows in the vow expressions that appear in the Torah.

for this is like a vow even though he did not express it in the language of a vow. The language of a vow is when he forbids something to himself, whereas here he takes upon himself to do something without mentioning vow or oath language, and therefore this is not a full vow.
just as he is permitted to eat them. Because one who vows by a forbidden thing, his vow does not take effect.
as we have explained. Above, halakhot 8-9.
so he is permitted with his wife. By the basic law (and see below 2:13 for how it is practiced).
"The enjoyment of your marital relations is forbidden to me". He forbids himself the enjoyment of marital relations with his wife.

she is forbidden to him, as will be explained. Below 12:9. For although he cannot forbid the act itself to his wife because he is obligated to her, he can forbid himself by a vow the enjoyment of the act (and see Hilchot Ishut 14:6, that in such a case he is compelled to divorce her after seven days).
whether he vowed of his own accord or his fellow bound him by a vow etc.. The law is the same.
or something that means the same as "amen". Such as saying "yes" and the like (compare Hilchot Shevuot 2:1).
as we explained in Shevuot. 2:10-12.
he is like one who swears with the mind of others. The hearts of others stand in place of his heart, and he cannot say that in his heart it was one way or another (Hilchot Shevuot 2:15).
within the time of speaking. The time to say the words "Peace upon you, Rabbi" (Hilchot Shevuot 2:17; see also there, halakhot 18-19).
for he nullified the condition in this vow. For he vowed even though the condition was in his mind.
and if he did not remember the condition until after he vowed. It seems that he forgot his condition but still desires it, and therefore the vow is void.

even though he accepted the condition in his heart and upheld the condition. Although when he remembered he did not express the condition with his mouth but only accepted and upheld it in his heart, the vow is void (Kesef Mishneh; see Radbaz and Meiri Ha-Kesef, who explained otherwise).

provided that he remembers the condition after he vowed within the time of speaking. For the vow is not nullified when the one vowing does not remember his condition at all, but only if he remembered the condition within the time of speaking and accepted and upheld it in his heart (Kesef Mishneh, in whose understanding there is no difference between this opinion and that of the Raavad). Some explain that according to this opinion it suffices that he remember the condition within the time of speaking, and there is no need for him to accept and uphold it in his heart (Lechem Mishneh).

if he said, "I am acting according to my first intention," his vow is not a vow, for he has nullified it. Although for one who remembers his condition at the time of the vow his vow stands, here, where he said that his vow is subject to a condition, the condition nullifies the vow.
he may put a condition before his oaths. He may do so if he wants to nullify his oaths in the future.

unspecified vows are treated strictly. Because presumably the intention of one who vows is to forbid something to himself (Rosh, Nedarim 18b); and some explain that it is like any doubt in Torah law, in which we are stringent (Kiryat Sefer; Tiferet Yisrael, Nedarim 2:4).
like salted meat of an offering and like wine of a libation that was poured on the altar. These are things made subject to vows by the person, and one who extends a vow by them, his vow is a vow.
offering of idolatry and wine poured for it. These are forbidden, and one who extends a vow by something forbidden, his vow does not take effect (above 1:8).
and if he vowed without specification. When asked about the intention of his vow, he answered that he vowed unspecifically, with no particular intention.
it is forbidden. Because unspecified vows are treated strictly.
if like the cherem of the Temple upkeep etc.. For there are two kinds of cherem: cherem for Temple upkeep, meant for the needs of the Temple, and cherem for kohanim (Hilchot Arachin VeCharamin 6:1).

it is permitted because it is their property. For after it comes to the kohen it is considered ordinary and the kohen's property (ibid. halakhah 5). Therefore he did not extend his vow by something forbidden but by something permitted, as if he had extended his vow by ordinary food.
as we have explained. Above 1:13.
and if like the tithe of grain, it is permitted. For terumot and ma'asrot do not come by vow or voluntary gift (as above 1:11).
if he meant the terumah of the chamber. The shekels given in the chamber and used to buy communal offerings (Hilchot Shekalim 4:1).
and if he meant the terumah of the threshing floor, it is permitted. For terumat hagoren is defined as a "forbidden thing" (as above 1:11).

and said there, "They are cherem upon me," it is forbidden. Even if the one vowing claims he meant the cherem of kohanim, his intention is not taken into account, but we follow the usual meaning of the words in that place and at that time (Kesef Mishneh).
which is a fishing net. A net of fishermen.
with the offerings of kings. Gifts presented before kings.
"I myself am a korban upon you". It can be understood as forbidding his benefit to his fellow like an offering (Commentary to the Mishnah, Nedarim 2:5).
with a bone that I set aside for myself. With a bone of an animal that he kept with him.
we show him that this is a vow etc.. We create in him that impression by seeking another reason to permit the vow and not releasing it on the basis of his intention.
for there is no vow here, as we have explained. Above 1:8, 1:30.

even though it is not a vow, it is like a vow in that it is forbidden to retract. But if he retracted within three days, although he is forbidden to do so, his retraction is a retraction (as below halakhah 17, see Derishah; and see Radbaz, who explained otherwise).
like the sabbatical year. Like the law of grain and fruit that grow in the sabbatical year, which are ownerless for all.
and one who declares his adult slaves ownerless. Canaanite slaves.
they acquired themselves. For adults have understanding, and therefore when he declares them ownerless they leave the master's domain and acquire themselves from the ownerless state.
and minors. Who lack understanding and therefore cannot acquire themselves.

whoever came first and took possession of it. Who performed an act of acquisition by chazakah on the land, for example by locking its entrance, fencing it, or widening a breach in it (see Hilchot Mechirah 1:8).
and he is exempt from the tithes, as will be explained in its place. Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 5:27; Hilchot Terumot 2:11.
by rabbinic law. By the words of the Sages.
and the two testify. That the person acquired it from the ownerless state.

for three days he can retract. And the field returns to his hands as the owner of the field and not as ownerless property, and he is not exempt from the tithes, as if he had not declared it ownerless (Lechem Mishneh; Perishah 273:3).

until he or another has acquired it, he can retract. Although with a plain declaration of ownerlessness he can retract only within three days, when he made a change and declared it ownerless for a set time, he can retract throughout that whole time, unless he or another has acquired it.
until he lifts it, if it is movable property. For movable property is acquired by lifting (Hilchot Mechirah 3:1).
or takes possession of the land. For land is acquired by chazakah, such as locking, fencing or breaching the land in any effective way (ibid. 1:8).

regarding an oath of utterance. An oath that a person swears about something that was or was not done in the past, or about something that he will or will not do in the future (Hilchot Shevuot 1:1-3).

an oath does not take effect on an oath. For example, if he swore not to eat this loaf and then swore again not to eat the same loaf, he is punished for only one oath (ibid. 4:9-10; for the reason for this law see the explanation there).
one who extends an oath is exempt. For example, if he heard his fellow swear and said, "And I like you," he is exempt (ibid. 2:8).
an oath of utterance applies only to optional matters. Matters whose performance depends on a person's will, but not matters that there is a commandment or prohibition to do (ibid. 5:14-16).

an oath of utterance applies to something with substance and to something without substance. The oath applies to the person himself and forbids him various actions, so he can forbid himself sleeping or speaking even though they are not substantive things. A vow, by contrast, applies to objects that become forbidden to a person, so he cannot forbid by a vow the performance of actions, since they are not substantive.

he is liable for each and every one. Specifically in vows of consecration, where he extended his vow by bringing an offering, a vow takes effect on a vow and he is liable for each one; but in prohibition vows, for example if he forbade himself a loaf and then forbade himself the loaf again, if he eats it he is liable for only one (Lechem Mishneh).
within the time of speaking. The time it takes to say "Peace upon you, Rabbi" (Hilchot Shevuot 2:17).
this one who said "and I". The second person who said "and I."

even after several days. For the forbidden object is before him and he extends it onto that, and therefore this extension is effective even after time. But in the previous case, where he says to his fellow "and I like you," the extension is effective only within the time of speaking, because afterward it is not clear that he means the vow his fellow made (Radbaz; Me'iri Ha-Kesef).
sitting in the sukkah on the festival is forbidden to him. For example, he forbade the sukkah to himself, and therefore he may not sit in it (Commentary to the Mishnah, Nedarim 2:2).

these are forbidden to him. Because by the vow the object became forbidden (as explained in the next halakhah), and now if he performs the commandment with it, it is a commandment fulfilled through a transgression (Commentary to the Mishnah, ibid.).
for the matters indicate this, as the Sages received from oral tradition. That the interpretation of the verses matches the Oral Torah tradition.
to do harm or to do good, optional matters. For matters placed in a person's hand to do or not to do are optional matters.
as we have explained. Hilchot Shevuot 5:16.
as we have explained. In the previous halakhot.

and it is a festival or the eve of Yom Kippur... and needless to say Rosh Chodesh. Although fasting on a festival is forbidden by Torah law (see Hilchot Ta'aniyot 1:7, 1:9; Hilchot Yom Tov 6:19), the vow takes effect. Likewise on the eve of Yom Kippur, when it is customary to eat in preparation for the fast of Yom Kippur, and on Rosh Chodesh, which it is customary to honor with eating and on which one does not fast (Hilchot Ta'aniyot, ibid.), if he vowed not to eat on them, the vow takes effect (see Kesef Mishneh and Aruch HaShulchan, Orach Chayim 604:6-8).

if Chanukah and Purim fall upon it, his vow is set aside because of these days. This applies specifically to a vow of an individual fast; but with a fast that the community took upon itself, although it is not set for these days to begin with, if they began fasting for a calamity and the like and these days fell upon them, they fast on them (Hilchot Ta'aniyot, ibid.).
and the prohibition of fasting on them is rabbinic. See Hilchot Ta'aniyot, ibid.; Hilchot Megillah VeChanukah 3:3.
they require reinforcement. The status of these days must be strengthened, so that people do not come to treat them lightly.
"my speech to you is a korban". Its meaning is: my speech is forbidden to you like an offering.
that I will not serve you. That I will not have marital relations with you.
the vow takes effect on them. For he forbade his mouth or his hands and the like, and these have substance.
he is liable for an offering. Although he made his vow depend on something without substance, in vows of consecration the vow takes effect.
and likewise if he vowed "I spoke" and "I did not speak". For example, he said, "An offering is upon me if I spoke," or "if I did not speak."
for these are not the prohibition vows whose laws we are explaining. The rules stated here concern prohibition vows and not vows of consecration (as above 1:1-3).

although the vow does not take effect on them, we do not instruct him to treat them as permitted. By Torah law the vow does not take effect, but the Sages forbade this vow because people consider it a vow (Commentary to the Mishnah, Nedarim 2:1), and therefore in this law there is no difference between a Torah scholar and an ignoramus (unlike above 1:27, 2:13; Kesef Mishneh, Radbaz, Lechem Mishneh; some hold that here too a Torah scholar needs no release; see Kesef Mishneh).

and vows made in error. For example, he said, "Konam, this loaf is forbidden to me if I ate and drank," and remembered that he ate and drank, or he said, "Konam, my wife may not benefit from me, for she stole my purse or struck my son," and it turned out that she did not steal or strike (as below 8:3-4; and see Hilchot Shevuot 3:6).
and vows of exaggeration. Hyperbole and nonsense. For example, he said, "Konam, this loaf is forbidden to me if I did not see so-and-so's army like those who left Egypt" (see Hilchot Shevuot 3:5).
in the manner we explained regarding oaths. Hilchot Shevuot 3:1-6.
the violent men. Violent men and robbers.
the tax collectors. Those who collect customs duty.
and even though he added to what they asked of him. For he did so to strengthen his words in the eyes of the violent man or the tax collector.

and relies on what is in his heart, since he is under duress and cannot express it with his lips. In other laws no force is given to the thought of the heart (see for example Hilchot Mechirah 11:9), but here we rely on it because of the duress.
as we have explained regarding oaths. 3:3.
who bound his fellow by a vow to eat at his house. The host forbade himself to benefit from his fellow if his fellow does not come to eat at his house.
and this one vowed not to eat. For example, he forbade himself to benefit from his fellow, or forbade his food to himself.
for a sela. Four dinars.
for a shekel. Two dinars.
and they agreed. They were appeased and agreed.

for a person is forbidden to vow with the intention of nullifying them. In vows of exaggeration and urging he must refrain from vowing, and in vows of error and duress he must try as much as possible to avoid reaching a situation in which he would need to vow (Aruch HaShulchan 232:40; Perishah 232:4).
and regretted. He regretted it.
asks. He goes to request release, and the sage asks him questions in order to release him.
and in the language in which they release an oath they release a vow. They say to him, "It is permitted to you," or "it is released to you," or "it is forgiven to you."
and likewise the other matters that we explained regarding oaths. Hilchot Shevuot, chapter 6.

and a vow is not released until it takes effect. For example, he vowed not to eat meat for thirty days from the first of Iyar onward and regretted it; he cannot ask about his vow until the month of Iyar begins and the vow takes effect.
like an oath. Hilchot Shevuot 6:14.
prohibition vows... vows of consecration. For their explanation see above 1:1-2.
consecrated property for the upkeep of the Temple. Things consecrated for the needs of the Temple.
consecrated property of the altar. Things consecrated for the needs of the altar.

and one cannot ask about an exchange offering. If a person said of his ordinary animal that it should be the substitute for his offering animal, the substitute too becomes sanctified, and he cannot ask to release his vow, because a substitute made in error is also sanctified (Hilchot Temurah 1:2), and the release of the vow reveals that the vow was in error, yet a substitute made in error is also sacred (Kesef Mishneh).
and just as a father or husband annuls prohibition vows. See below 11:6 ff.

so he annuls vows of consecration that resemble prohibition vows. For just as one asks about both, so one annuls both (and each of them can annul what he is entitled to annul among prohibition vows; see below 12:1; R. Y. Kafah).
and his fellow heard and said, "And I". And the vow takes effect on him as with one who extends a vow (above 3:3).
all are released. For their vow is an extension dependent on the first vow.
and he extended the meat. He said, "This meat is like this bread" (as above 3:4).
it is released with respect to the meat. For the prohibition of the meat is an extension dependent on the prohibition of the bread, and the bread was released.
for it was released from its whole. That part of it was released.

"to this one and to this one and to this one" - if the first was released, all are released. Because he used the connecting "and" there is a single inclusion, and thus an extension of one onto another (Lechem Mishneh).

"I do not benefit from this one, this one, this one" - each one needs a separate opening. Because he did not use the connecting "and" and specified each separately, it is as if he vowed on each one separately, and there is not a single vow.
he vowed by nazirite, by offering and by oath. For example, he forbade himself a food by oath and added that if he eats it he will be a nazirite and liable for an offering.
or he vowed and it is not known by which of them he vowed. Whether by naziriteship, offering or oath, and he must act stringently regarding all of them because of the doubt.

one opening for all of them. Since he accepted them together, there is a single vow, and if one of them was released, all are permitted, because a vow part of which was released is entirely released; and all the more so when he acted stringently regarding all only out of doubt, one opening releases them.
one who vows from the people of the town. He forbade himself to receive benefit from them.
and asks the sage of the town. Although ab initio he may not ask him about his vow (below 7:9).
or one who vowed from Israel. He forbade himself to receive benefit from all of Israel.
and he asks a sage of Israel. Even ab initio, since he has no other option.
a decree, lest he go tomorrow to that place. And it would turn out retroactively that the fruits he ate were forbidden to him.
and if he did not go, he is not flogged. Although he violated a rabbinic decree, one is not flogged for it.
he completes the fast. Although he forgot and ate, when he remembers he continues the fast that day, since he vowed specifically this day (see also Hilchot Ta'aniyot 1:14).
he is not flogged, for Shimon said nothing. Therefore he does not violate "he shall not profane his word."
as we have explained. Above 2:1.
even if he gave it to him as a gift, it is forbidden to him. For the one who bound him by vow gave it to the one bound directly.
or another gave it to him as a gift. The owner of the loaf gave it to someone, and that person gave it to the one bound as a gift.

for he said to him only "my loaf". Although he said "this one," since he said "my loaf," it is forbidden to the one bound only while it is in the possession of the one who bound him or comes directly from him to the other; but once it has left the possession of the one who bound him and then reached the one bound, it is permitted to him.
even though he sold them. To another person (see also below 8:11).
or he swore that he will not benefit from him. When a person swears that so-and-so will not benefit from something in his possession, the oath binds that person (Hilchot Shevuot 5:4).
he shall not inherit it. Although he acquires the property (and therefore may give it to his brother or his sons, as in halakhah 8 below), it is forbidden to him in benefit (Kesef Mishneh).
and the grandson is permitted in them if he is a Torah scholar. That is, that the property is acquired by him even though his father himself is forbidden in it (see Kesef Mishneh).
and he must inform them that "these are my father's assets, which he forbade to me". So that he not benefit from the money forbidden to him (Commentary to the Mishnah, Bava Kamma 9:11).

for one who swears that his fellow shall not benefit from him is permitted to pay his debt, as will be explained. Below 6:4, that paying the debt of the one bound is not direct benefit but only removal of a claim, and therefore he may pay his debt or pay his wife's ketubah from the money forbidden to him.
he is permitted with the permitted kinds even though they have the taste of the forbidden kind. For he forbade himself only that kind as it is and not its mixture or its taste.

if they have the taste of the forbidden, they are forbidden. Since he forbade himself these specific fruits, they became like a forbidden thing, and therefore if they are mixed in, their taste forbids.
and if not, they are permitted. Like the law of a forbidden thing mixed with a permitted one, which when it has no taste of the forbidden is permitted (Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 15:6).
because he can ask about his vow. That he can ask about his vow, and then it will be permitted to drink the wine.

it became like a thing that has permitters, which is not nullified in its own kind, as we explained in Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot. For something that has permitters is not nullified when mixed with its own kind, even in thousands times its amount. But if it is mixed with something not of its kind, it is nullified (Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 15:10-12).

in their exchanges. If he exchanged the forbidden fruits for something else or for money, their exchanges too are forbidden, because he made them like consecrated property, whose exchanges also become forbidden (Meiri, Nedarim 57a; Ran, ibid.).
and in their growths. If other fruits grew from them, they are forbidden.
and needless to say the liquids that come out of them. For the liquid is closer to the fruit itself than the exchange, and even than the growth.
whose seed is consumed when sown. Its seed is consumed and decays before it sprouts.

he is permitted in their exchanges and their growths. For he forbade himself only eating and tasting them, and in the exchanges and growths nothing of the substance or taste of the forbidden fruit remains.
even the growths of their growths are forbidden. For some substance or mixed taste of the forbidden fruit remains in them.

liquids that come out of them are in doubt. It is in doubt whether he meant to forbid the fruits themselves but not the liquids that come out of them, or whether the liquids too are included in the prohibition.
as we explained. Above, halakhah 12.

their growths and their exchanges are in doubt. For a person cannot forbid his fellow's fruits to his fellow because they are not in his possession, and therefore we are in doubt whether he is able to forbid the growths and exchanges of his own fruits to his fellow, since these too are not yet in existence and so are not in his possession (Babylonian Talmud, Nedarim 47a).
a sifter. A utensil for sifting flour.
and a sieve. A utensil for sifting grains of produce and seeds (Commentary to the Mishnah, Shevi'it 5:9).
millstones. Used for grinding.
food. Human food.
he lends him. The one who forbade to the one forbidden.

and it is forbidden to borrow from him a sack to bring him fruit or a donkey to bring fruit on it. Although these are not utensils with which food is prepared, they serve to transport food and cause the benefit of food.
it is forbidden to borrow from him even utensils with which food is not prepared. For he saves him the rental fee, and with that money he can buy food, so this is a benefit that leads to food.
to be seen with them in front of others, until he benefits from them. For example, he borrows from him fine clothes or jewelry, and through this they will give him good food at the banquet.
in order to go to a place where he will benefit. Food benefit, for example passing through the courtyard of the one forbidden in order to go to the house where food is served.
one forbidden benefit from his fellow. Who forbade his fellow's benefit to himself or whose fellow forbade his benefit to him.
stepping on foot. Passing through his courtyard and the like, which is forbidden to one forbidden benefit but permitted to one forbidden food.
through him. On his behalf.
the half-shekel. Every Israelite man is commanded to give a half-shekel each year to fund the communal offerings of the coming year (Hilchot Shekalim 1:1).

and preventing a claim is not included in prohibitions of benefit. The prohibition is to give the forbidden person actual benefit, and in preventing damage or preventing a claim for a debt nothing came into the hand of the forbidden person, and it caused him only satisfaction (see Commentary to the Mishnah, Nedarim 4:2-3).
whether impure. For even though he does not eat it, fattening it will raise its price when he sells it.
for the kohanim are emissaries of Heaven. They are commanded to offer the sacrifices by the Holy One, blessed be He, and they are His emissaries.
they are not the emissaries of the owner of the offering. Thus he does not give Reuven benefit.
the adult woman. A girl who has turned twelve and has shown signs of maturity is called a na'arah, and six months after that she is called a bogeret (Hilchot Ishut 2:1-2).
with her consent. For being an adult, he cannot marry her off except with her consent (ibid. 3:12), and therefore Shimon does not give Reuven benefit by this (Radbaz).

but if she was a na'arah, for she is still in his domain, it is forbidden. For as long as she is a na'arah, her father has the authority to betroth her to whomever he wishes (Hilchot Ishut, ibid. halakhah 11).
with his knowledge. For one cannot separate terumah or tithes without the owner's consent (Hilchot Terumot 4:2).
whoever wishes to separate terumah may come and separate it. So the terumah is with his consent, but in a way that he did not appoint him as an agent.
for it is forbidden to take payment for it. As explained in Hilchot Talmud Torah 1:7, so he does not save him tuition and does not give him benefit.
but not the Written Torah, for which one may take payment. For payment may be taken for it (ibid.), and therefore if he teaches him for free he saves him the tuition and gives him benefit.

he may teach his son. Although a father is obligated to teach his son (ibid. 1:1), and thus he relieves him of a commandment that rests upon him, this is not real benefit but the prevention of effort (similar to paying a debt, as above halakhah 4).
and he teaches him Oral Torah. For free.
Shimon enters and visits him. Because visiting the sick is a commandment (Hilchot Evel 14:1).
to keep him company. To be with him.
Shimon may not sit. For he saves him the payment of a visitor's fee, and thus gives him benefit.

for this is a commandment. A doctor is obligated to heal the sick of Israel, as it says regarding returning a lost item, "and you shall return it to him," and the Sages explained that even if he sees him lost through bodily illness, it falls within this commandment to restore his body to health, with his body, his money or his knowledge (Commentary to the Mishnah, Nedarim 4:4).
Shimon may not heal it. For he is not commanded to heal his fellow's animal.
but he says to him, "Do such and such to it". For giving advice itself involves no real benefit.
when he raises the water on him. In a small bath, the one who enters raises the water level.
and reclines with him on the couch. At the meal, since such sitting involves no warming benefit (Ran, Nedarim 41b).
and they eat at one table. And we do not worry that they will eat from each other's food.
from a trough set before workers. A hollow filled with fruit from which all the workers eat (Commentary to the Mishnah, Nedarim 4:4).
it is permitted, and we do not worry that he set aside a good piece for him. Because the host will refill the dish before serving it to Reuven (ibid.).
a cup of consolation. A cup of wine that was customarily drunk in the house of a mourner (see Hilchot Evel 13:8).
from the hand of Shimon of Reuven's. The cup belongs to Reuven and Shimon hands it to him.
and likewise the cup of the bathhouse. They used to bring hot water to one coming out of the bathhouse for healing (Rosh, Nedarim 38b; see Hilchot De'ot 4:17).
for there is no benefit in this. For the cup is Reuven's and Shimon only hands it to him.

and Reuven is forbidden Shimon's coal but permitted his flame. Because a coal has substance, so there is benefit from a substantive thing, whereas a flame has no substance (see also Hilchot Avodah Zarah 7:10).
the olive press. The place where oil is produced from olives.
a hold of the hand. A right of use (Commentary to the Mishnah, Nedarim 5:3).
he rented it. He leased it.
the press basket. A round basket of ropes into which olives are put to produce oil.
he rented everything. He leased everything to the lessee.
it is permitted. For he does not benefit from Shimon but from the lessee.
even in the sabbatical year, when everything is ownerless. For in the sabbatical year the owners of fields are commanded to declare ownerless everything the land produces (Hilchot Shemitah 4:24).

for he vowed before the sabbatical year. And one who forbids his property to his fellow with the words "these assets" and the like, they are forbidden to his fellow even after they leave his possession (as above 5:5; and see the next halakhah).

but if he vowed in the sabbatical year, he may eat from the fruits that hang outside the field. For in the sabbatical year the fruits are not in Shimon's possession, and the vow does not take effect on them.

a decree lest he remain there after he eats. Lest he linger in the field after he finishes eating the fruits, and one forbidden benefit from his fellow may not stay in his field, since stepping on foot is forbidden to him (as above halakhah 3).
and the Torah made it ownerless only as long as the fruits are in it. For the field itself is not ownerless but only for the eating of the fruits in it (Commentary to the Mishnah, Nedarim 4:5).
in what case is this said. That if he vowed before the sabbatical year, the fruits are forbidden to the one bound.
for they have left Shimon's possession. And he forbade them to him only while they are in his possession (as above 5:5).
for the reason we explained. In the previous halakhah.
he may go down into his field. For one forbidden food from his fellow is permitted to step on foot in his field (as above halakhah 3).
and if they became forbidden in the sabbatical year, he may go down and eat. For the vow does not take effect on the fruits, and one forbidden food may remain in the field after the fruits are gone.

and he may not sell to him, a decree lest he buy from him. Even in cases where the forbidden person does not benefit from the sale (for example, he sells to Shimon cheaply), they forbade him to sell to him out of concern that he might later buy from him cheaply and thus benefit from him (and see below 7:7).
a decree lest he assist him. For example, he reaps near him, and his fellow who is bound finds free space in which he can walk to do his work (Commentary to the Mishnah, Nedarim 4:4).
and these things are not considered regarding the son. Since these are not special tasks but small tasks that a father usually does for his son, presumably the father did not mean them when he vowed.
or vowed not to speak with his fellow. For example, he said, "My mouth is an offering for speaking with you," or "My mouth is forbidden for your speech," and the like.
for if he takes payment, he turns out to benefit. The returner, from the payment for returning.
and if he does not take, he turns out to give benefit. The returner gives benefit to the owner of the lost item, since he saves him the payment for returning.

and they are permitted in things that are jointly owned by all of Israel. Although every Israelite has ownership in these things, since it is a very small share, we do not worry about it (Commentary to the Mishnah, Nedarim 5:4).
and the well in the middle of the road. Which serves those going up to the festival pilgrimages (ibid.).
and they are forbidden in things jointly owned by all the people of the town. Because their share in it is not small, we worry about it (Meiri, Nedarim 47b).
the town square. The town marketplace.
and the ark. In which the Torah scroll is placed (Hilchot Tefillah 11:3).
and the books. Used for study and prayer.
he writes his share to the prince or to one of the rest of the people. He writes a document by which he removes his ownership from his share and grants it to the prince or to another person.
partners in a courtyard. Whose houses are adjacent to one another, and the houses have a shared courtyard.

if it is subject to the law of division. When four cubits remain in the shared courtyard for each partner (aside from the four cubits each has across the width of his entrance), they divide it among them (Hilchot Shecheinim 2:1). And as long as they have not divided it, it is not known where each one's share is, so he benefits from his fellow's by entering the courtyard.
each one enters his house. Through the courtyard.
and he says, "I enter into my own". Since division is impossible, and when they used it before, each was permitted to use all of it, so too they may use it after they forbade each other.

both are forbidden to set up a mill, an oven, or to raise chickens in this courtyard. Because ordinary partners can prevent one another from doing these things (ibid. 5:3), he benefits from the fact that his partner does not prevent him.
two who were partners in a courtyard. Which is not subject to the law of division.
that the second not benefit from it. That his partner not benefit from it.

we compel the one who vowed to sell his share. For by his vow he causes his partner to stumble if he uses the courtyard in a forbidden way (for example, by setting up an oven and stoves), and therefore we force him to sell his share.

he vowed that he himself not benefit from the second, he may enter his house, because he enters by his own right. And we do not worry that he will stumble by setting up an oven and stoves, since a person is careful about the prohibitions of benefit he took upon himself.
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 4.
he may enter this courtyard. Specifically a courtyard that is not subject to the law of division; but if it is subject to the law of division, another may not enter until they divide it (Radbaz).
to buy from them at a higher price and sell to them at a lower price. Than the accepted price, so that he does not benefit from them since he does not profit.
if they listen to him to buy at less and sell at more. Even though they would lose, and therefore it is reasonable that they will not listen to him.
and we do not decree here that he not sell, lest he buy. As they decreed regarding one forbidden benefit from his fellow (above 6:16).

for if he cannot do business with this one, he will do business with another. This is the reason why when he vowed from one person we decree, but when he vowed benefit from a whole nation and there is no other option, they did not decree.
it is forbidden to ask about his vow from a sage of that town. For he receives benefit from him in the very act of release.
his vow is released. Although he benefited from this sage, the release stands and the vow is void (Kesef Mishneh; see Lechem Mishneh).
as we explained. Above 4:13.

with leket, shikhchah and pe'ah. Various portions of the field's produce that are given to the poor (see Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 1:1-6), which do not belong to the owner but have the law of ownerless property for the poor, and therefore he may benefit from them.

and the poor man's tithe that is distributed on the threshing floors but not that within the house. A tithe given to the poor in the third and sixth years of the sabbatical cycle (ibid. 6:1-4). When it is distributed from the threshing floor, the owner of the field must give to every poor person who comes to take, and therefore there is no favor in it. But when it is distributed at home, he may give it to whichever poor person he wishes, and therefore there is a favor in it and it is forbidden to the one bound (see there, halakhah 10).
their gifts. For example, the terumot and tithes given to them.
against his will. And it is not considered that they receive benefit from him.
these are forbidden. Since he can give them to another kohen or Levite, if he gives to these who are forbidden to him there is a favor in it.

and the same law applies to gifts to the poor with respect to the poor. That if he forbade his benefit to all the poor, they come and take from him against his will. And if he forbade his benefit to certain poor people, he gives to other poor people (and this applies specifically to the tithe distributed at home, as above halakhah 10; Me'iri Ha-Kesef).
and came and took from this one. The shopkeeper came and took the money from the one who bound him by vow.
it is permitted. For the one who bound him by vow is paying the debt of the one bound (Commentary to the Mishnah, Nedarim 4:7, and as explained in the next halakhah).
and we have already explained. Above 6:4.
he gives it to another as a gift. And thereby the item is acquired by that person, and the one bound is permitted to benefit from it.

he places it on the rock and says, "These are ownerless". Although by rabbinic law one must declare ownerless in the presence of three, since by Torah law one may declare ownerless even before one, in this case they set it on the Torah law (Shach 221:53; see above 2:16).

this is forbidden. Because it is evident that giving the meal as a gift is only so that the one bound can come eat with the one who bound him (and in the previous halakhah they permitted because he has nothing to eat).
for his meal proves about him that he did not intend to transfer ownership to him. For a person does not prepare a large meal and transfer ownership of it to another.

for if he consecrated it, it would not be consecrated, it is not a gift. For example, in the case in the previous halakhah, if the recipient of the gift consecrated the meal he received, it would not be consecrated. Therefore this is not a gift, and the one bound may not benefit from it (see Mishnah Nedarim 5:6).

and anyone who gives a gift to this one in order to transfer it to another etc.. For example, in the case mentioned, where the one who bound him by vow gave the meal as a gift to so-and-so on condition that he give it to the one bound, so it is not acquired by him except on condition that he transfer it to the one bound. Since the recipient has no way to acquire the gift for himself but only to give it to the one bound, the gift comes to the one bound directly from the one who bound him, and it is forbidden to him to benefit from it. Some explain that this speaks of a case where he forbade the first to benefit and transferred to him on condition that he transfer to another (like the example mentioned above in 5:7). And if the first did not transfer to the second, the first did not acquire because he is forbidden to benefit, and the second did not acquire because the condition of the transfer was not fulfilled, as with anyone who gives a conditional gift, where if the condition is void the gift is void (Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 3:6; R. Y. Kafah).

one whose benefit was forbidden to his daughter's husband. And if her father gives her a gift, the husband will acquire the fruits of the gift (as below; and see also Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 3:12), and thus he gives him benefit.
he gives to her and says to her etc.. In these ways the husband does not acquire at all (ibid. halakhot 13-14).
died. The dog or the father.
short. Low.
my purse. My wallet.
and came into being. Newly arose.
a scribe. The town scribe responsible for writing documents.

even though he says, "If I had known etc.". The vow is not released by this statement, because he has not yet regretted his wish not to benefit from so-and-so, but would have preferred that he not be a scribe so that he would not have to benefit from him.
until he releases his vow as we explained. Hilchot Shevuot 6:12, that a vow is not released through a new development unless the one vowing regretted his vow.
since his father is permitted. For he did not intend to forbid this to his father.

"If I had known, I would have said: so-and-so and so-and-so are forbidden and my father is permitted" - all are permitted. For he changed the language of the vow; at first he said, "They are an offering upon you," and at the end he said, "So-and-so and so-and-so are forbidden and my father is permitted," and thus part of the first vow was released, and therefore all of it was released.

for he revealed his mind that he did not release part of the vow, but would have vowed as he did and stipulated regarding his father. For he did not change the language of the vow but only added a condition to it, and thus part of the vow was not released but a condition was added to it.
if he said, "If I had known, I would not have vowed". He has nullified the whole vow, and he is permitted in everything.

even if he said, "If I had known, I would have said: the new is forbidden and the old is permitted" - he is permitted in the old and in the new. Part of the vow was released, and therefore all of it was released.
he is permitted only in the old. For the vow was not released but a condition was added to it.
the whole meaning of the statement. The literal meaning.
and to cover themselves. To cover himself with them.
to throw them behind him. To load them as a burden on his back.
and it is permitted to cover oneself with fleeces of wool. Which are not spun like a garment.
for he intended only a wool garment. In the manner of wearing, but did not intend to forbid himself to cover himself with wool as a covering.
one who refuses. Who refuses.
and they pressed him. They urged him, tried to persuade him.
but for the sake of marriage. Not to marry them.
this is forbidden. For he forbade the house to himself regardless of its ownership (see also above 5:4-5).
swore or vowed. The borrower, out of anger at his fellow who refused to lend to him (Rashi, Nedarim 43a, and others).
with his hand. By his own efforts.

he is forbidden, and all people are permitted to plow for him with it. For he intended to forbid only according to his custom of plowing himself, but did not forbid plowing the field with this cow by others.
he shall set out. He shall sail.
until he finds a matter that is fitting for him. According to what is suitable and proper for him, and he is not obligated to do these things in every way that offers itself.
that he propose to her. That he propose to her to marry him.

and to the boiled. Lightly cooked in water without spices (R. Y. Kafah; see his note to the Commentary to the Mishnah, Berakhot 6:8, and Commentary to the Mishnah, Terumot 10:11). Some explain that shaluk means cooked thoroughly (Rashi, Nedarim 49a and others; see Meiri there, who says the word is explained in both senses, according to context).

and likewise smoked and cooked in the hot springs of Tiberias etc.. Food that was not cooked over fire but by smoke or in hot spring water. [Note: the Rambam in the Commentary to the Mishnah vocalizes this word Tevarya.]
we follow the language of the people of the town. If their way is to call these methods "cooked," it will be forbidden in them.
to all salted foods. Any food that was soaked or seasoned with much salt.
to consult about it. To consult with the one who sent him whether to buy this kind in place of the kind he was sent to buy.

it is included in the kind that was told to the agent without specification. The kind about which it is customary to consult is included in the original kind told to the agent, and therefore if he vowed from the original kind, he is forbidden also in the kind about which one consults.
and everywhere. Even in a place where the agent does not consult about these things.
he is forbidden poultry meat. For poultry meat is included in the category of meat more than fish meat (for the reason see Kesef Mishneh and Lechem Mishneh).
and entrails. The inner parts of the animal; although their quality is lower compared with the main parts of the meat, they are included in the category of meat.
and he is permitted locusts. Which are not a kind of meat.
until it congealed. It solidified and became hard.
but only rolled. Lightly cooked in hot water and still soft.
one who vows from a pot-dish is forbidden only things that are brought to a boil in a pot. That do not require much cooking but only boiling.
rifot. Cooked grain that is dried and ground, and boiled in a pot.
and levivot. Dough that is boiled in a pot (see Hilchot Berakhot 3:4).
with tzir. The liquid drained from salted fish (Commentary to the Mishnah, Nedarim 6:4).
and with fish muries. Muries is a seasoning made of various things, and here it speaks of muries made of fish (ibid.).
one who vows from wheat is forbidden it both raw and cooked. For the term
. "chittim" refers to wheat in its kernels, whether he eats them raw or cooked, but he is permitted flour and bread.

"wheat, wheat that I do not taste" - he is forbidden both flour and bread. For the term "chittah" refers to the product of wheat, whether ground or baked. And when he said "chittah chittim," he added to the prohibition of raw and cooked these forms as well.
"wheat that I do not taste" - he is forbidden it baked. And this includes also cooked flour.
and it is permitted to grind it. And this includes also cooked wheat kernels (see Merkevet HaMishneh).
from the five kinds. Wheat, barley, spelt, oats, rye.
one who vows from vegetables is permitted gourds. For vegetables means vegetables eaten raw, and gourd is not eaten raw but cooked, and therefore it is permitted (Babylonian Talmud, Nedarim 54a).

from leeks is permitted kaflotot. Different kinds of leeks, and kaflotot is a kind of leek that grows in the Land of Israel (see Commentary to the Mishnah, Kilayim 1:2; Ma'aser Sheni 2:1 and R. Y. Kafah's notes there).
the water of cooked vegetables is like the cooked vegetables. The water in which the vegetables were cooked is like the vegetables themselves and is forbidden (compare Hilchot Berakhot 8:4).

he vowed from the water of cooked vegetables, he is permitted the cooked vegetables themselves. For the cooked vegetables are primary and therefore the water follows them in prohibition, but the water does not drag the cooked vegetables after it.
the grisin. Ground beans.
in a mikpeh. In a stew.
and he is permitted truffles and mushrooms. Which in the language of people are not defined as fruits of the earth because they have no roots by which they draw from the ground.
although they do not draw from the ground, they grow in the ground. For mushrooms sprout from the ground, and therefore in the language of people they are defined as products of the ground.
he is forbidden all the fruits of the year. Both tree fruits and ground fruits until the end of the year.
he is forbidden only figs. For figs are cut by hand and therefore are called "kayitz," unlike other fruits that are cut with a tool (Babylonian Talmud, Nedarim 61b).
even the new. Although the taste of new wine is similar to the taste of grapes.
the sitvaniyot. Autumn grapes that are not fit for eating and from which vinegar is made.
from field vegetables. Those that grow wild in the fields.
for all these are secondary names. An added name that is not the primary meaning of this name, and he intended to vow from the primary meaning.
the garment. A garment.
in sackcloth. A fabric of hair (Commentary to the Mishnah, Nedarim 7:3).
and in a yeri'ah. A thick unsewn garment, woven in coarse weave (ibid.).
and in a chamilah. A wrap that was customarily made thick and coarse and served to cover the head against rain (ibid.).
he is forbidden the upper room. In the house on the second floor.
for it is like a small bed. And this bed is placed before the large bed to ease climbing onto the large bed (ibid. 7:5).

from the threshold inward. From the place where the door is closed inward (Commentary to the Mishnah, Nedarim 7:5), but he is permitted in the thickness of the threshold outside the place where the door closes.
to its boundary. The two thousand cubits around the city that are considered the city's boundary, beyond which one may not go on Shabbat (Hilchot Shabbat 27:1-2).

and it is forbidden to enter its ibbur. The area added to the city when houses located about seventy cubits (about 35 meters) from the city are joined to it, and the boundary is measured from them onward (see Commentary to the Mishnah, ibid.; Hilchot Shabbat 28:1).
and stayed there twelve months... thirty days. For further consequences of these definitions see Hilchot Shecheinim 6:5; Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 9:12.
those that draw from it. That are above it and its water seeps under the ground and wells up in them.
those that are drawn. That are below it and its water flows into them.
and they are not accompanied by the name of the spring that was vowed. The name of the original spring is not used as an accompaniment to the name of these.
those who sail. Those who travel by sea.
the blind. Blind people.

he vowed from the black-headed, he is forbidden the bald and the gray-haired etc.. Because the expression "black-headed" refers to people who sometimes cover their heads and sometimes uncover them, unlike women, whose hair is always covered and who are called "covered of head," and unlike children, whose heads are always uncovered and who are called "uncovered of head" (Ran, Nedarim 30b).
he vowed from Sabbath-resters, he is forbidden Israelites and Cutheans. Samaritans, who were careful to observe the Sabbath.
for he intended only one who is commanded to go up to Jerusalem. And the Samaritans do not go up on pilgrimage to Jerusalem but to Mount Gerizim.

and Isaac said to Jacob, "May He give you the blessing of Abraham". From which it follows that Jacob is the continuation of Abraham's seed (see also Hilchot Melachim 10:7; see Commentary to the Mishnah, Nedarim 3:11, who gives another reason).
until it grows dark. For this is the end of the day.
from time to time. A full day from the time of his vow.
this week. This week.
for the rest of the days of the week. The days of the week remaining from the time of his vow onward.
seven days from time to time. A week from the time of his vow.
as we explained. In the previous paragraph.

even if it was a deficient month. Although in a deficient month there are about twelve and a half hours that belong to the current month but are included in the next month (see Hilchot Kiddush HaChodesh 6:1-2), nevertheless since in practice they are part of the next Rosh Chodesh, he is permitted in them (R. Y. Kafah; see Radbaz, who explained otherwise).
a full year from day to day. Until the same date in the following year.

and if the year was made a leap year, he is forbidden in it and in its added month. If an additional month was added to this year and now it has thirteen months, he is forbidden in all of them, because the cycle of a full year is until the same date in the following year.
as we explained. Above, halakhah 2.
a shavua. A cycle of seven sabbatical years.
a yovel. A cycle of seven sabbatical cycles ending in the fiftieth year.

and if he vowed until the end of Adar, he is forbidden until the end of the second Adar. Even if he did not know that the year is a leap year, when he says the end of Adar, he means the end of any month that will be called Adar.
and if he knew that the year is a leap year and vowed until the beginning of Adar, he is forbidden until the beginning of the second Adar. For he means any Rosh Chodesh that will be called Adar.
he is forbidden only until it arrives. And on Pesach itself he is permitted.
anything whose time is fixed. Such as Pesach.
and vowed until it. For example, he said, "until Pesach."
the kayitz. The summer days; and in their time this name was well known for the season of ripening of figs, when they start to be eaten (Commentary to the Mishnah, Nedarim 8:4; see above 9:12).
fig baskets. Baskets in which the cut figs are placed.

until the people begin to reap the wheat harvest, but not the barley harvest. The barley harvest is earlier than the wheat harvest, and the wheat harvest is called simply "the harvest" in the language of people.
that they fold. That they fold up.
the mats. On which fruits are spread to dry, and after the gathering of the fruits they are folded until the next year.
in the muktzeh. The name of the place where fruits are spread.
dried figs. Dried figs.
and he went up to the mountain. And summer comes sooner in the valley than in the mountain.

he is forbidden until the time of the rains, which in the Land of Israel is Rosh Chodesh Kislev. The descent of rains at the beginning of winter has three pulses called "revi'ot" (Babylonian Talmud, Nedarim 63a). For vows, the determining revi'ah is the second, because rains that fall before it are rains of the end of summer and not of the beginning of winter (see Babylonian Talmud there and Commentary to the Mishnah, Pe'ah 8:1). However, the time of this revi'ah varies by the type of year: in an early year, the 17th of Marcheshvan; in a middle year, the 23rd of Marcheshvan; in a late year, Rosh Chodesh Kislev (ibid.). When he vowed "until the rain," even if no rain actually fell, his vow ends at the second revi'ah of a late year, since this language includes the arrival of the rainy season even without rain falling.
and if the rains fell from the seventeenth of Marcheshvan. Which is the second revi'ah in an early year.
it is permitted. For the language "until the rain" also means actual falling of rain, from the second revi'ah in an early year (see Commentary to the Mishnah, Nedarim 8:3).

and if he said "until the rains," he is forbidden until the rains fall... from the twenty-third of Marcheshvan onward. For the meaning of this language is actual falling of rain, and we interpret his intention as the falling of rain at the second revi'ah of a middle year.
until Pesach passes in the Land of Israel and in places like it. For this is the time when the rains stop in the Land of Israel and its surroundings.
she is forbidden to benefit from him immediately, a decree lest she go. And if she goes, it turns out retroactively that every benefit she gave him before was forbidden.
he is flogged. But the woman is not flogged, like Reuven who bound Shimon by vow, where although Shimon is forbidden to benefit from Reuven, if he benefited he is not flogged (as above 5:1).
even though the condition has passed. Although he made the prohibition of benefit depend only until Pesach, and Pesach has already passed.

he may not treat his vow as permitted and let her go and benefit. He is obligated to prevent her from going until the festival, for her going, while she benefited from him before, causes the benefit that she gave until Pesach to have been forbidden (Kesef Mishneh).

and if she went after Pesach, she is not forbidden to benefit from him. Even if she benefited before Pesach, and by her going after Pesach she caused him to violate his prohibition retroactively, nevertheless she is not forbidden to benefit after Pesach, as that is not within his vow.
and she is forbidden his benefit until the festival. For she went to her father's house before Pesach.
and she is permitted to go to her father's house once Pesach has arrived. For the period of prohibition in the condition of the vow has ended.

a minor boy of twelve years and one day and a minor girl of eleven years and one day etc.. Although a male is not called an adult until he reaches thirteen years and one day, and a female until twelve years and one day, and they show signs of maturity (Hilchot Ishut 2:1, 2:10), and before this time they are considered minors whose acts have no legal force (see for example ibid. 4:7), for vows their law is different, as will be explained.
if they knew in whose name they vowed. That the one who vows vows in the name of Heaven, as it says: "When a man vows a vow to the Lord" (Numbers 30:3).

and if they did not know, their words are nothing. Although they are not liable, they are compelled to keep their words in order to educate them not to treat vows lightly. And if it is a vow whose fulfillment would harm the minor, he is not compelled to fulfill it, but his father or teacher strikes him and rebukes him so that he does not become accustomed to treating vows lightly (see Hilchot Shevuot 12:7, that even before this age this is the practice; Me'iri Ha-Kesef).
and they require examination throughout the entire year. As explained in the next halakhah.
and they asked them. Whether they know in whose name they vowed or consecrated.
before this time. Before age twelve for a male and eleven for a female.
and even though they did not grow two hairs. And in other matters, before they grow two hairs, their acts have no legal force.
and this is the time of vows mentioned everywhere. For vows and consecrations (see Hilchot Nezirut 2:13; Hilchot Arachin 1:15; Hilchot Terumot 4:5).

and this matter is from the words of the Torah, for the mufla who is near to being a man etc.. The Sages learned from the extra word "ish" (man) in the verse "ish ki yafli" that a minor who has reached the age of maturity but has not shown signs, and is near to being called a man, if he vowed ("yafli"), his vow is a vow and his consecration is a consecration (Babylonian Talmud, Nazir 62a). But the period in which the vows of a boy and girl are examined is rabbinic (Tzafnat Pa'neach, Shabbat 24:11; Responsa Igrot Moshe, Even HaEzer 170).
they swore and changed. They swore a false oath or swore and did not fulfill their oath.
they are not flogged until they grow up and grow two hairs. For a minor is not subject to punishment until he grows in years and shows signs of maturity (see Hilchot Mamrim 7:5).
he is flogged. Like any person who eats consecrated property, who is flogged (Hilchot Me'ilah 1:3).
as we explained. Above, halakhah 4.

even if she became an adult and is a na'arah. A girl who has reached twelve years and one day and shown signs of maturity becomes an adult and is called a na'arah for six months (Hilchot Ishut 2:1-2).

her father annuls her vows etc.. The Torah gave the father authority to annul the vows of his daughter in the na'arah years if he expresses disapproval on the day he hears the vow (for a description of the manner of annulment see below, chapter 13).
on the day he hears it. He may annul until the end of the day on which he heard her vow (below 13:15-16).
all her vows and prohibitions. And the continuation of the verse:

". "that she has bound upon her soul shall not stand, and the Lord will forgive her, because her father restrained her," so the father has the power to prevent her from fulfilling the vow by annulment.
she became an adult. That six months have been completed after she became a na'arah (see the explanation in a previous halakhah).

a husband annuls the vows of his wife and her oaths. For the Torah gave the husband authority to annul vows of self-affliction or vows about matters between him and her that his wife vowed (as below 12:1).
once she enters the chuppah. From the time the husband brings her into his house and is alone with her, from which time the woman is defined as married (Hilchot Ishut 10:1).
she was divorced in doubt. For example, he threw her the get in such a way that it is doubtful whether it reached her (see Hilchot Gerushin 5:13).
he gave her a get conditionally or after a time. That he made the get depend on the fulfillment of a certain condition or said that it takes effect after a certain time (see ibid. 8:1, 9:1).
and likewise one who heard that her husband died and married, and her husband is alive. In such a case she must be divorced from both and is forbidden to marry them forever (Hilchot Gerushin 10:5).

and likewise anyone similar to her. Anyone whose betrothal does not take effect with her, such as one of the women forbidden to him by the prohibitions of forbidden relations (see Hilchot Ishut 4:12), he cannot annul her vows.
if she was among those liable under a prohibition. For example a widow to a High Priest or a divorcee to an ordinary priest (for more examples see there 1:7).
and needless to say among those liable under a positive commandment. For example an Egyptian or Edomite convert (see there 1:8).
these can have their vows annulled. Because betrothal takes effect with a woman who is forbidden to him by a prohibition or a positive commandment (ibid. 4:14).
a betrothed young woman. Who was betrothed to her husband but has not yet entered the wedding canopy.
the husband. The betrothed.
she does not receive lashes. Since the betrothed's annulment lessens the severity of the vow, even though it is not annulled, she does not receive lashes for it.
if the betrothed died, she returns to her father's authority. Only while she is still a minor or a young woman; but after she reaches adulthood, her father does not annul her vows.
and any she vows. After her betrothed died (as for what she vowed before he died, see below halachah 16).
for a husband does not annul his wife's vows until she enters the wedding canopy. The betrothed cannot annul alone, even when the father is not alive.
and her betrothed did not hear. If her betrothed did hear, see below halachot 15-17.
on that day. For the annulment of vows is only on the day the vow is heard (as below 12:17).

her father and her last husband annul her vows that she made when she had the first betrothed. Since the first betrothed did not hear, the possibility of annulling passes from betrothed to betrothed up to the last betrothed, who joins the father in annulling on that same day (and if she was not betrothed again, the father can annul alone - as below halachah 16).

because she did not leave her own authority for even a moment, for she is still in her father's authority. Since she was divorced from betrothal, she returns to her father's authority. But if she was divorced from marriage, she left her father's authority (below halachah 25).
since she went into her own authority in the interim, her vows stand. For after a woman is divorced, her husband does not annul her vows (above halachah 8).

even after several days, when the father and the last betrothed hear, they annul her vows. The annulment of vows is on the day of hearing and not necessarily the day of the vow (below 12:16). This applies only when they heard on the same day; but if they heard on separate days, they cannot annul (ibid. halachah 17).
since the first betrothed did not hear them. And see below halachah 17 for the law where the first betrothed did hear.

her father and her last betrothed annul her vows. For the last betrothed takes the place of the first betrothed, and the father can annul together with him. But the father alone cannot annul (as below halachah 19).
her father together with the last betrothed annul her vows. As explained in the previous halachah.
she became vacant. She returned.
the father cannot annul. For the betrothed upheld it, and even his silence until the next day is an upholding (below 12:18).

and the father annuls together with the last husband to whom she is betrothed that day. And by the same token, if she was not betrothed again, he can annul alone in this case (as above halachah 16, Lechem Mishneh).
even if the husband heard before the father died. And if he had annulled at that time, it would have been annulled.

a betrothed heard and annulled for her, etc.. In contrast to the cases mentioned above in halachah 16, where the father can annul alone after the betrothed's death, here the case is that one of the parties heard and annulled, and afterwards the betrothed died before the other party heard; in these cases the father cannot annul alone.
as we have explained. Above halachot 14-15.
until she entered his authority. Until she married him.
therefore. Because of the cases detailed just above (halachot 18-20) in which a situation arises where the vows cannot be annulled.

that a husband annuls his wife's vows even though he did not hear them. And likewise the father, for the father too annuls with the words "all vows you have vowed in my house" (Lechem Mishneh, below 12:13). Some explain that the father cannot annul without hearing, and that what he says, "all vows you vowed...," is meant to cause her to tell him so that he can annul (Perishah 234:40).

the father went with the husband's agents, or the father's agents went with the husband's agents. When a father hands over his daughter for marriage after she was betrothed, as long as the father himself or his agents are with her, she has not yet left her father's authority and is still considered betrothed (see Hilchot Ishut 22:1-2).

the father handed her over to the husband's agents, or the father's agents handed her over, etc.. When the young woman is handed over to the husband or his agents without the father or his agents going along, the young woman enters her husband's authority.
