nor can the husband annul, for a husband does not annul prior vows. A husband does not annul the vows of his betrothed after she entered his authority; but if she vows from here on, he can annul (Kesef Mishneh).
as we have explained. Above halachah 20.

a woman awaiting yibbum. A woman whose husband (from betrothal or from marriage) died without children and who is waiting for one of his brothers to take her through intercourse (yibbum) as the Torah commanded (Hilchot Yibbum VeChalitzah 1:1).
a ma'amar. A rabbinic betrothal in which the yavam betrothes his yevamah before witnesses with a perutah or something worth a perutah (ibid. 2:1).
even one yavam and one yevamah. Where the deceased husband has only one brother, who is the only one commanded to perform yibbum.
does not annul the vows of his yevamah until he has intercourse with her. For by Torah law she does not enter his authority except through intercourse.
if his yevamah was a young woman betrothed to his brother. Who was betrothed to his brother but had not yet married him, and he died.

but only the father alone annuls whatever she vows. Like the law of a betrothed young woman whose betrothed died, who returns to her father's authority, and he alone annuls her vows (above halachah 16).

for a ma'amar does not acquire the yevamah with a complete acquisition. As long as the yavam has not taken her through intercourse, she has not entered his authority and is still in her father's authority.
as we have explained. Hilchot Yibbum VeChalitzah 2:1.

she is like an orphan in her father's lifetime. For when he married her off she left his authority, and when she was divorced or widowed she does not return to his authority but is in her own authority (Hilchot Ishut 3:12), and the same applies to a minor (ibid.).
until she reached adulthood. Until six months passed after she became a young woman; from this age her father does not annul her vows (as above halachah 7).
who became an orphan in her father's lifetime. For example she was widowed from marriage and left to her own authority, and afterwards was betrothed.
for he annuls together with him in partnership. The father and the betrothed annul in partnership, and when she left her father's authority, the betrothed alone cannot annul.
on the day he heard it. And not afterwards (as below halachah 15).
affliction of the soul. Physical suffering, as the Torah explicitly says, "Every vow and every sworn oath to afflict the soul, her husband may uphold it and her husband may annul it" (Numbers 30:14).
between her and him. Those that relate to the relationship between him and his wife.
that she would not paint her eyes. That she would not put blue makeup on her eyes.
that she would not adorn herself. With colorful clothes.
as it is said, between a man and his wife. The Sages learned that besides vows of affliction of the soul, he can also annul vows between him and her (Babylonian Talmud, Nedarim 79b).
she vowed not to eat meat. A vow that involves affliction of the soul.
she forbade to herself relations with any man in the world. This includes forbidding relations with him, and this is a vow between him and her.
he annuls his part. The prohibition of relations that applies to him.

and likewise if she vowed not to paint her eyes today or not to wear embroidery. These are vows between him and her (as above halachah 1, Lechem Mishneh), and even in these, if she vowed for a short time, he may annul.
even if she vowed to abstain from bad food, etc.. A vow that causes her not to eat some food, if she should wish, is considered affliction of the soul.

for one there is affliction and for one there is no affliction. For example, one is fine bread, which if she does not eat she will go hungry, and the other is black bread, which if she does not eat she will not go hungry. Or if she eats one of them she will be full, so there is no affliction if she does not eat the second (Rashi, Nedarim 82b).
to bother. To make the effort.
not to benefit from people. From people.
even though the husband is not included. He is not included in the vow, as he is not among "people," and she is permitted to benefit from him (Babylonian Talmud, Nedarim 83b).

and likewise if she forbade benefit from her whole nation. That she forbade herself to benefit from them; he annuls because this is a vow involving affliction (Commentary to the Mishnah, Nedarim 11:12).
he does not need to annul. Because the wife is obligated to serve him.
with the rest of the clothing and conjugal rights. For a man is obligated to provide for his wife's food, clothing, and conjugal relations.
as we have explained in Hilchot Ishut. 12:2.

the pleasure of your relations is forbidden to me. Although she cannot forbid the act of relations itself, she cannot engage in them without deriving pleasure, and she can forbid the pleasure to herself (and see also above 1:30, that a husband can forbid himself the pleasure of his wife's relations).
let my hands be consecrated to their Maker. Her intention is to consecrate her hands to the Creator, so that whatever she does with them will be consecrated.
because her hands are pledged to him. For the Sages enacted that the work of a woman's hands is pledged to her husband in return for her sustenance (Hilchot Ishut 12:4).

even though they said that emancipation, chametz, and consecration remove a lien, etc.. If a borrower pledged his slave, his chametz, or his property as security for a loan, and afterward freed his slave, or Passover arrived, or he consecrated his property, in all these cases the lien lapses (see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 18:6, Hilchot Chametz UMatzah 4:5, Hilchot Arachin VaCharamin 7:14). Although by this logic a wife's consecration should have removed the lien on the work of her hands to her husband, the Sages reinforced their own enactment more than Torah law, and consecration does not remove this lien.

but he must annul, lest he divorce her and she be forbidden to return to him. If he does not annul and then divorces her, the lien on the work of her hands to the husband lapses and the vow takes effect, and he will not be able to marry her again, lest he stumble and benefit from the work of her hands.
and likewise if she vowed, "I will not give water to your animals or straw to your cattle". A wife is not obligated to do these things for her husband (see Hilchot Ishut 21:5).

the husband and the father may annul vows that have not yet taken effect and by which she is not yet forbidden. In contrast to the release of a vow or oath by a sage, which cannot be done before it takes effect (Hilchot Shevuot 6:14), a father or husband annuls even before the vow takes effect (but he cannot annul in advance vows she has not yet made, below 13:9).
who cannot hear. Deaf people.
even though a husband annuls vows he did not hear. And likewise the father (Lechem Mishneh). Some explain that the father cannot annul vows he did not hear (Perishah 234:40; and see above 11:21).
one who is able to hear is not held back by not having heard. But a deaf person is not able to hear, and therefore cannot annul.
he does not annul. Because the actions of an imbecile have no legal force.
a minor has no husbandhood. For his betrothals are not betrothals (Hilchot Ishut 4:7; and see also there 11:6).
the whole day, and not twenty-four hours. Until the end of the day on which she vowed, and not a full day from the moment of the vow.
he annuls all that night and all the next day. For the day begins with the night and ends at nightfall on the following day.
and what is this that is written in the Torah, "from day to day". One might understand that the annulment of the vow is a full twenty-four hours.

to teach that he annuls at night if she vowed at night, and likewise he annuls all day. From the verse "on the day he heard it" one might think the annulment is only by day and not at night; therefore it says "from day to day," to teach that throughout that whole day one may annul (Babylonian Talmud, Nedarim 76b).
as we have explained. In the previous halachah.
and her husband heard on the day he heard. Just as the first "day he heard" is the day the father heard, so the "day he heard" mentioned here is the day the father heard (Lechem Mishneh).
and how do we know that the verse speaks of a betrothed young woman. For the verse says, "if she is to be a man's," and one might understand that it speaks of a married woman.
and if she vowed in her husband's house. There the verse speaks of a married woman.
and they give her stripes for rebelliousness. Lashes by rabbinic law.

she is liable for what she transgressed - lashes if lashes, and a sacrifice if a sacrifice. In this annulment differs from release: when a person violated his oath or vow and then asked a sage, who released him, he is exempt from a sacrifice or lashes (Hilchot Shevuot 6:18), because the sage's release cancels the vow altogether, whereas annulment uproots the vow from the moment of annulment onward (see below 13:2 for explanation).
in any language. In any tongue.
who does not recognize. Who does not understand.

"I do not want you to vow" or "there is no vow here" - he has not annulled. For she has already vowed and there is a vow here, unlike "this vow is nothing," in which he admits there is a vow and annuls it (Radbaz).
"It is forgiven to you," "It is permitted to you," or "It is released to you". These are the expressions of release of a vow by a sage (Hilchot Shevuot 6:5).

for the father and the husband do not release like a sage, but uproot the vow from its beginning and annul it. This wording is difficult, because Rambam's language here implies that the father or husband uproots the vow retroactively (and this is implied also from the Commentary to the Mishnah, Nedarim 10:8). However, the Gemara's conclusion (Nazir 21b) is that it is the sage who uproots the vow retroactively, whereas the husband annuls only from now on ("a sage uproots, a husband cuts"), and so Rambam too explained (Commentary to the Mishnah, Nazir 4:1), and so it emerges from many laws in these halachot, for example: one who violated his vow and the sage then released him is not liable (Hilchot Shevuot 6:18), whereas a woman who violated her vow before her husband annulled it for her is liable (above 12:19; Hilchot Nezirut 9:11); and likewise one who linked his vow to someone else's vow and then the sage released it, the linked vow too is void (above 4:9), whereas one who linked his vow to a woman's vow and then her husband annulled it, the linked vow is not void (below halachah 15). See Lechem Mishneh and other commentators who struggled to reconcile Rambam's wording with the Gemara and the above laws.
that he say to them. To his wife or his daughter (some versions: "that he say to her").
go. You (feminine).
to utter with his lips. To say it aloud.

vows may be annulled on the Sabbath, whether for the needs of the Sabbath or not for the needs of the Sabbath. Although a sage releases vows only for the needs of the Sabbath (Hilchot Shevuot 6:6), since the annulment must be done on the day of hearing, even vows that are not for the needs of the Sabbath are annulled (and see also Hilchot Shabbat 24:6).

as it is said, "her husband may uphold it and her husband may annul it". From here we learn that the husband himself upholds or annuls. From this verse we also learn that the husband can annul only a vow that has come into force, but not a vow that has not come into force, such as one she has not yet made (Mishnah, Nedarim 10:7).
as is said regarding release. That a vow partly released is entirely released (above 4:11).
and included himself in her vow. For example he heard and said within speaking time of her vow, "and I" (see above 3:3).
for he has upheld it for her. From his including himself in her vow, we understand that he wants her vow, and it is considered an upholding.
and decided in his heart to bind her by a vow. That he bound her by his vow absolutely and not doubtfully.
he cannot annul. For it is clear that he wants her vow, and it is considered an upholding.

and if he annulled hers, his is void, since it is as if he made his vow dependent on hers. Since he annulled her vow, his vow too is void (see Rabbi Kapach; and see the commentators who labored to explain this halachah according to a different text that was before them in Mishnah Nazir 4:2).

and the one who included himself is liable. Since the husband's annulment does not void the vow but uproots it from the moment of annulment onward, the husband's annulment does not uproot the inclusion that the vower made while the woman's vow was in force, unlike a sage's release, which voids the vow entirely so that even the vow of the one who linked himself is void (above 4:9; and see above halachah 2 for explanation).

and the vow of a widow or divorcee - all that she has forbidden to herself. The Sages explained that this refers to a woman who vowed before she married: even if the vow takes effect after the marriage, the husband does not annul her vow; rather "all that she has forbidden to herself shall stand against her" (see Commentary to the Mishnah, Nedarim 11:9).
for a husband does not annul prior vows. Vows that preceded the marriage.
as we have explained. Above 11:20.
as we have explained. Above halachah 7.
within speaking time. The time it takes to say the words "Peace upon you, my teacher" (Hilchot Shevuot 2:17).

so that the power of things in the heart will not be greater than the power of one who utters with his lips. Just as one who explicitly utters with his lips can retract within speaking time (as above 2:3), so too one who upholds in his heart.
